builder_plan.scenario: You already need task-specific training and want to reduce its memory or compute cost.
builder_plan.change: Change only the training technique on a small controlled run after checking prerequisites.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current training recipe with the same model, data split, and evaluation.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Held-out quality, peak memory, training time, and full compute cost to the target quality.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: RASP: Read-All, Sparse-Plasticity Continual Learning in a Stationary-Size LoRA
summary: RASP replaces per-task LoRA branch expansion and symmetric sparse MoE gating with a single fixed-size LoRA in which inference reads all rank-1 atoms at full rank while a cosine router restricts gradients to a top-q sparse subset, stabilized by a Gram-coherence penalty and a geometric consolidation index. The cost is additional routing and consolidation bookkeeping in the backward pass, task-boundary anchor locking logic, and implementation complexity well beyond a standard LoRA fine-tune. It can fail when tasks do not share a compatible low-rank feature space, when router channel selection misaligns with new-task inputs, and the reported gains are confined to ViT image-classification benchmarks rather than generative or language workloads.
rationale: The method addresses continual fine-tuning of vision transformers under a fixed memory budget, which suits constrained infrastructure, but its value depends entirely on whether the reader actually runs sequential-task vision workloads, so adoption should be conditional on workload-specific validation.
technique: Stationary-size LoRA continual learning via sparse plasticity

claims.statement: RASP replaces per-task LoRA branch expansion and symmetric sparse MoE gating with a single fixed-size LoRA in which inference reads all rank-1 atoms at full rank while a cosine router restricts gradients to a top-q sparse subset, stabilized by a Gram-coherence penalty and a geometric consolidation index. The cost is additional routing and consolidation bookkeeping in the backward pass, task-boundary anchor locking logic, and implementation complexity well beyond a standard LoRA fine-tune. It can fail when tasks do not share a compatible low-rank feature space, when router channel selection misaligns with new-task inputs, and the reported gains are confined to ViT image-classification benchmarks rather than generative or language workloads.

RASP matches or surpasses branch-expanding LoRA continual learners on CIFAR-100, CUB-200, ImageNet-R, and ImageNet-A while keeping a strictly constant adapter parameter footprint instead of one LoRA branch per session.
